newsitem.title: USA: US House panel upholds $270 mln cap on EEP in FY98.
newsitem.headline: US House panel upholds $270 mln cap on EEP in FY98.

text.p: A key House panel on Wednesday approved a $270 million spending cap on the U.S's main export subsidy program in fiscal 1998 despite a world trade agreement that would allow much more.

The House Appropriations Committee took the action without strong protest from the Clinton administration, which earlier this year had requested $500 million for the Export Enhancement Program--the maximum amount allowed by the 1996 farm act.

Due to strong markets and tight U.S. and world grain supplies, the U.S. has not subsidized wheat and most other eligible commodities under EEP for nearly two years. That left the program vunerable to cuts when appropriators faced a funding dilemma for the federal crop insurance program.
The $270 million cap on EEP was first approved three weeks ago by the House appropriations subcommittee on agriculture.

On Tuesday, USDA Secretary Dan Glickman told reporters that he would prefer to see more funding for EEP but understood that the appropriations panel faced a difficult task funding the crop insurance program.
Congress initially approved $100 million for EEP in fiscal 1997, but cut that to $10 million earlier this summer to help pay for Northern Plains flood assistance.
Meanwhile, there are signs that USDA might reactivate the program for some commodities in the near future.

Glickman confirmed Tuesday that the Clinton administration is reviewing whether to resume export subsidies for wheat flour and barley malt because of a sharp drop in U.S. exports of those commodities in recent years.

He noted that conditions were "not ripe" yet for a resumption of export subsidies for bulk commodities such as wheat and barley, but added that could change depending on the size of crops around the world and other factors.
Under the Uruguay Round trade pact, the U.S. committed to reduce export subsidy spending by 36% and export subsidy volume by 21 percent over a six-year period beginning in 1995.
Even so, the U.S. could spend $524 million just on wheat export subsidies in fiscal 1998 and still be within its Uruguay Round committments.

For other export program, the House Appropriations Committee approved just under $1 billion for international food assistance under the PL480 program and $5.7 billion in export credit guarantees to help countries finance purchases of U.S. farm goods.
The full House is expected to take up the agriculture program spending bill in the coming weeks, clearing the way for the Senate to work on it version of the legislation.
